rows.selection_reason: With no prior evidence, I need to establish a strong baseline while testing the most impactful design axes simultaneously. Config_050 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) combines the strongest prior choices: scgpt (purpose-built single-cell foundation model for RNA), imagenet_vit_l (state-of-the-art vision encoder), transformer aggregation (most expressive for multiprofile), and weighted fusion (learnable combination of modalities). This tests whether the full multimodal pipeline with top-tier encoders and expressive aggregation/fusion can achieve high validation accuracy. If it performs well, it sets a strong bar and I can ablate components in later experiments. If it underperforms, subsequent experiments can isolate which component (encoder choice, aggregation, fusion) is the bottleneck. Given only 10 experiments for 51 configs, starting with the highest-prior configuration maximizes the chance of finding a strong solution early while still providing diagnostic information about the design space.

Evidence: config_050 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieved 52.0% accuracy / 47.9% F1, but with only one data point I cannot tell whether the image modality, the transformer aggregation, or the weighted fusion is actually contributing beyond what the RNA encoder alone provides. Question: config_010 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, transformer) is the cleanest single-variable ablation of config_050—it keeps the same RNA encoder (scgpt), same profile setting (multiprofile), and same aggregation (transformer), removing only the image branch. Why this is the best next experiment: establishing the RNA-only baseline is the highest-information experiment at this stage. If RNA alone approaches ~52%, the remaining 8 experiments should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation improvements and the image modality is deprioritized. If RNA alone is substantially lower (e.g., <45%), multimodal fusion is confirmed as a key lever and I should invest remaining budget in fusion strategies and image encoder choices. This single comparison partitions the search space efficiently and prevents wasting experiments on a modality combination that may not be the bottleneck.

The two completed experiments (config_050: multimodal/weighted, acc=0.520; config_010: RNA-only, acc=0.514) show only a marginal accuracy gain from adding the image modality, while F1 actually drops, suggesting the fusion strategy may be suboptimal. Config_040 is identical to config_050 except it uses concat fusion instead of weighted fusion, providing a clean single-variable ablation. This directly tests whether the weighted fusion is the bottleneck or whether a simple concatenation of modality representations performs comparably or better. Resolving this question early is critical: if concat outperforms weighted, it opens a clear exploitation path across other encoders; if they are similar, the fusion choice is not the limiting factor and I should pivot to testing alternative RNA encoders (pca_n2000, scvi_n200) in the remaining budget. With 7 experiments left, isolating this one variable now maximizes information per experiment.

The current best (config_050, acc=0.520) uses transformer aggregation with weighted fusion, scgpt, and imagenet_vit_l. The only other aggregation tested (in config_040) was also transformer with concat fusion, which underperformed. We have no evidence yet about whether avgpool aggregation could match or beat transformer in the multimodal multiprofile setting. config_019 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to the current best, changing only aggregation from transformer to avgpool. This is the best use of the next experiment because: (1) it directly tests a fundamental architectural choice with minimal confounding, (2) if avgpool performs comparably, it validates a simpler/faster architecture and frees later experiments to explore other dimensions (RNA encoder, image encoder), and (3) if it underperforms, it confirms transformer aggregation is critical and we can focus remaining budget on encoder and profile choices. With 6 experiments left, reducing uncertainty on this core design axis early is more valuable than jumping to a less-tested dimension.

The best result so far is config_019 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.542 accuracy, clearly establishing that avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion outperform transformer/concat for this multimodal setup. The remaining uncertainty is whether the specific RNA encoder (scgpt) is optimal for complementing the image features, or whether a different encoder like SCVI (a VAE-based latent representation) would interact more effectively with the imagenet_vit_l image features. Config_026 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) holds the three best-performing design choices (avgpool, weighted, imagenet_vit_l) constant while swapping the RNA encoder to SCVI, which captures a fundamentally different latent space (variational posterior) than scgpt (generative model). This is the most informative single-variable extension of the current best: if SCVI matches or exceeds scgpt, it opens a new direction; if it falls short, it confirms scgpt as the preferred RNA encoder and lets us focus remaining budget on other axes. With 5 experiments left, this targeted test maximizes information gain about the RNA encoder dimension without risking the already-validated aggregation/fusion/image-encoder choices.

The dominant finding is that switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 (config_026 vs config_019, all else identical) produced a massive accuracy jump from 0.542 to 0.706, making scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted the clear best configuration. The most important untested dimension for this winning combination is the aggregation strategy: avgpool vs. transformer. With scgpt, avgpool was marginally better (0.542 vs 0.520), but the scvi_n200 latent representation may interact differently with transformer attention, potentially capturing cross-profile dependencies that simple pooling misses. config_027 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable change from the current best, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can push accuracy beyond 0.706. This is the highest-value experiment because it either confirms avgpool as optimal (reducing uncertainty and focusing remaining budget on other axes) or discovers a new best configuration, and it is the most natural logical extension of the strongest evidence in the search.

The strongest evidence shows scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_027, 0.725 acc) is the best configuration so far. With scgpt, weighted fusion consistently outperformed concat (0.520 vs 0.507 for transformer; similar gap expected for avgpool). However, the scgpt→scvi_n200 shift was so large (~0.20 acc) that the relative ranking of fusion strategies could plausibly differ. Config_017 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is the single most direct exploitation of the best config, testing whether concat fusion might match or exceed weighted in the scvi_n200 regime. If it does, it opens a new direction; if not, it confirms weighted is optimal and lets us redirect remaining budget to image encoder (resnet50) or profile setting. With 3 experiments left after this, resolving the fusion question early maximizes the information value of the remaining trials.

The strongest evidence shows scvi_n200 as the dominant RNA encoder (0.725 vs ~0.52 for scgpt), with transformer+weighted as the best aggregation/fusion pair (0.7250 for config_027). The one major untested variable in this top region is the image encoder: all top results use imagenet_vit_l, but resnet50 has never been paired with scvi_n200. Config_015 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether the image encoder choice meaningfully affects performance when the RNA encoder and architecture are already optimal. If resnet50 matches imagenet_vit_l, it confirms we've found the plateau and the final experiment can focus on fine-tuning; if it lags significantly, it validates imagenet_vit_l as essential and rules out that direction. With only 2 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information experiment: it either confirms the current best is near-optimal or opens a new avenue, making it the best use of the next slot.

Evidence: The top-4 results are all scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer, with config_027 (vit_l, weighted) at 0.7250 as the best. Notably, config_015 (resnet50, transformer, weighted) achieves the highest F1 (0.6945) despite lower accuracy (0.7131), suggesting resnet50 captures complementary information. The one untested combination in this proven region is resnet50 + transformer + concat (config_021). This tests whether concat fusion interacts differently with resnet50 than weighted does, potentially closing the accuracy gap to vit_l. With only 1 experiment remaining after this, this is the highest-EV exploitation: it stays in the best-performing architecture family, tests a genuinely new interaction (resnet50×concat), and if it underperforms, the last experiment can pivot to an alternative (e.g., config_034 or a singleprofile variant) with clearer information about which axis to explore.

The strongest evidence shows scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile is the dominant combination (best: config_027 at 0.725). We have three of four cells in the aggregation×fusion 2×2 matrix for this combination: transformer+weighted (0.725), transformer+concat (0.721), avgpool+weighted (0.706). Config_034 (avgpool+concat) completes this matrix, clarifying whether the interaction between aggregation and fusion is purely additive or if there's a specific synergy. While it is unlikely to surpass 0.725, it is the most logically informative remaining test within the proven best-encoder regime, and as the final experiment it closes the design gap with minimal risk of wasting budget on a structurally inferior setting (e.g., singleprofile or pca_n2000).
